records.name: Tennessee
records.current_summary:
Tennessee is the only US state with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere children could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable: the Sixth Circuit revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so its constitutionality has never been decided on the merits; no prosecutions are publicly reported, but a civil-rights suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event remains ongoing, and a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure rather than a dead-letter law.

Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters, and its ban on gender-affirming care for minors was constitutionally upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2025. Killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

sources.claim: LegalClarity (26 May 2026): the Adult Entertainment Act (2023, SB 3/HB 9) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — explicitly including 'male or female impersonators' — on public property or anywhere a child could see it; first offence is a Class A misdemeanour up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine, a second violation a Class E felony (1–6 years, fines to $3,000); it survived federal challenge on procedural grounds with a Supreme Court petition denied.

Advocate: the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to Tennessee's drag ban, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 Adult Entertainment Act in place; a separate suit remains ongoing, with performers saying they refuse to be silenced.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Tennessee's killing rate of trans women runs at 7.8 per 100k per year (10 recorded deaths, 2008–2025, undercount floor) and the state is graded in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier — the record's comparative-violence figure rests on this piece.

freshness_all.fact: Drag-act SCOTUS litigation upheld the law; 2025-06-18 Skrmetti upheld minor-care ban; 2026 'Riley Gaines Act' adds birth-sex placement in prisons (and shelter ban) - facility claims current and expanding.

records.name: Kansas
records.current_summary:
Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings, voids Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers (licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified), and creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.

Two trans men sued within days of enactment (Doe v. State of Kansas, with civil-liberties counsel), citing fear of violence under the law; a May 2026 injunction covers only the healthcare provisions, leaving the facility and ID regime in force.

sources.claim: ACLU of Kansas SB 244 FAQ: the law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities with new civil and criminal penalties; bars updating driver's licences or state IDs and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex at birth — the Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Erin in the Morning legal-risk assessment (20 Feb 2026): Kansas escalated Worst Laws -> Do Not Travel — the first 'Do Not Travel' state added in a year — driven by the new bathroom-bounty law letting private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities; directly the assessment this record quotes on interstate-travel exposure.

records.name: Mississippi
records.current_summary:
Mississippi enacted public-facility bans in 2024 and 2025 and defines legal sex by birth in statute, placing it in the worst-law group of the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading.

One institutional counterweight is documented: a federal court sentenced the killer of a trans woman in Lucedale to 49 years for a bias-motivated murder — evidence that violence here can meet real prosecutorial response even while hostile law stands.

sources.title: Trans Teen Cannot Change Name, Mississippi Supreme Court Rules - Mississippi Free Press
sources.claim: Mississippi Free Press/AP (23 Apr 2025): on 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act - which bans both surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors - as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest. Dated state-court confirmation of Mississippi's judicial posture on gender-transition recognition.

sources.title: Anti-Trans Bathroom, Sex Bills Die in Mississippi Legislature - Mississippi Free Press
sources.claim: Mississippi Free Press (1 May 2024): two anti-trans bills died in the Mississippi legislature after House and Senate lawmakers failed to reach agreement on compromise versions by the 29 April 2024 deadline - the 'SAFER Act,' which would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories (and which a House majority had previously supported), and the 'Women's Bill of Rights,' which would have codified a binary definition of sex as determined at birth into state law and curtailed legal recognition of transgender people's gender identities. Dated evidence of the 2024 legislative attempt at adult facility and sex-definition restrictions in Mississippi, which did not pass that session.

sources.title: Safe States Don't Make People Safer - The Needle
sources.claim: The Needle (16 Jul 2026), a state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women (per 100,000 trans women per year, 2008-2025, adjusted for undercounting): for Mississippi it records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 annually, above the US general-population homicide rate of 6.0 per 100,000 which the article prints as a comparison line; the piece's headline finding is that law tiers do not sort violence - both worst-law and safest-law states carry high rates. Gives the record a dated violence-rate datapoint for Mississippi, distinct from the state's legal-risk tier.

sources.title: Birth certificate bill restricting transgender Oklahomans heads to the governor - KJRH 2 News Oklahoma
sources.claim: KJRH 2 News Oklahoma (6 May 2026): House Bill 1225, which would require a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibit any changes with very little exception, headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk after passing its most recent vote 70-17. Authors said it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed the bill clarifies that Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes; critics called it further discrimination. Dated local coverage of Oklahoma's sex-at-birth document law while still pending the governor's signature.

For this record it confirms the two enactment years (2022 and 2025) behind Oklahoma's facility-use restriction.

records.name: Indiana
records.current_summary: A February 2026 per-state legal-risk assessment placed Indiana 'among the harshest anti-trans states in the country', citing its 2026 identity-document law and escalating bathroom restrictions as the drivers of its adult-risk rating; the July 2026 edition keeps it in the worst-state group.

sources.claim: Erin In The Morning 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map' (February 2026): per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law; states that Indiana's 2026 ID policy 'now places it among the harshest anti-trans states in the country', with bathroom-ban escalation driving adult risk and Kansas added to the 'Do Not Travel' category.

sources.title: Indiana bans driver's license gender changes despite public pushback
sources.claim: Indiana residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licenses or other identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles' new ban took effect on Feb. 1, 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement. The ban culminates an administrative rule change the BMV initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents. The article also reports that pending Indiana Senate Bill 182 would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons. This is the state's 2026 identity-document law the record ties to Indiana's harshest-state rating.

sources.title: Indiana Senate backs bill restricting transgender school restroom use
sources.claim: On Jan. 27, 2026, Indiana Senate Republicans approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House; the bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on their reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women 'continue to have their private spaces'; opponents including GenderNexus argued that letting anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement. This documents the escalating bathroom restrictions the record cites as a driver of Indiana's adult-risk rating.

sources.title: Indiana Supreme Court denies birth certificate gender change in split ruling
sources.claim: In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates; the denials left appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. This is the court outcome that kept Indiana's birth-certificate gender-marker change off limits ahead of the 2026 identity-document law.

sources.title: HB 1522 - Overview | North Dakota Legislative Branch
sources.claim: North Dakota Legislative Branch overview of HB 1522 (2023): an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code 'relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student,' with a penalty provision and an emergency clause. The page records the 2023 regular-session progression and the final disposition — governor signed, with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on May 9, 2023. This is North Dakota's enacted 2023 transgender-student statute, relevant to the record's account of state anti-trans legislation.

sources.title: Identity Document Laws and Policies - Movement Advancement Project
sources.claim: Movement Advancement Project's identity-document policy tracker states that North Dakota's 2023 law 'bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery', calling it a stricter, more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a 'negative law' state in its map. This supports the record's placement of North Dakota among states restricting birth-certificate gender-marker changes.

sources.title: Gov. Larry Rhoden signs anti-trans bathroom bill HB 1259 into law in South Dakota | Argus Leader via Yahoo News
sources.claim: Reports that Gov. Larry Rhoden's office announced on Friday, March 21, 2025 that he signed House Bill 1259 the previous day, restricting trans people from using bathrooms matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings. The measure takes effect July 1, 2025 and marks the first time in state history that any similar anti-trans bathroom bill has made it onto the books, after similar legislation failed in 2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022. For this record: primary-outlet confirmation of the signing date, bill number, scope and effective date of South Dakota's 2025 facility ban.

sources.title: A South Dakota Bathroom Bill Could Force Trans Inmates Into Solitary Confinement | Them
sources.claim: Detailed reporting on the vehicle behind South Dakota's 2025 facility restriction: House Bill 1259, which passed the state House by a 49-21 vote and would limit restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in state-run facilities to the same 'biological sex,' primarily targeting K-12 schools and state colleges including off-campus activities. The article documents how the bill's 'reasonable accommodation' clause and floor debate raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement to comply. For this record: bill number, House vote margin and the institutional scope (including prisons) of the law signed in March 2025.
